exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: A production schedule with cues, owners, dependencies, and contingency notes.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional ninety-minute community workshop has one host, one facilitator, and one venue contact. The schedule is a working production document for the people delivering the session.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Time: 12:30 · Cue: Room ready · Owner: Venue contact · Check: Seating and display checked
Time: 12:45 · Cue: Doors open · Owner: Host · Check: Welcome point staffed
Time: 13:00 · Cue: Opening remarks · Owner: Host · Check: Facilitator ready
Time: 13:10 · Cue: First exercise · Owner: Facilitator · Check: Materials on tables
Time: 14:15 · Cue: Closing discussion · Owner: Host · Check: Next steps visible
Time: 14:30 · Cue: Room reset · Owner: Venue contact · Check: Equipment returned
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Before doors open: Walk the room, check the display from the back row, and confirm who can make a timing decision. Keep the contact sheet private and available to the delivery team.
If a session runs late: Protect the closing time and shorten discussion before removing the break or access buffer. The host communicates the change clearly rather than silently pushing every later cue.
If equipment fails: Continue with the printed exercise and verbal instructions. A useful workshop should still work when the display is unavailable. Record any incident that affects the next event.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: schedule layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching portrait document PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
